utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-02- 60/2-S, the Prosecutor versus Dragan Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, ladies and gentlemen. For the sake of the record, may we have the appearances, please, for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Peter McCloskey, Stefan Waespi, and Janet Stewart for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. For the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, I'm having some difficulty with the earphones. David Wilson and Dusan Slijepcevic for the Defence. We are getting an awful lot of static. We're not sure why.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you. You may sit down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Obrenovic, can you hear the proceedings in a language that you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Do you have anything to complain concerning of the Detention Unit?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I have no complaints.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. This is a sentencing hearing for Mr. Obrenovic in accordance with the Rule 100 of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence, as well as the scheduling decision made by this Chamber on the 10th of October, 2003. This Trial Chamber has received the sentencing briefings by both parties, as well as the supplemental submissions by both parties. So to begin with, I would like to invite the parties to brief us on the highlights of their submissions to this sentencing hearing. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. As Your Honours are fully aware, we're here today because Mr. Obrenovic has stood up and taken responsibility for his actions and pled guilty, and we are here today pursuant to that plea and the plea agreement. I want to make it clear now that the Prosecution believes that Mr. Obrenovic has fully cooperated with the Prosecution, and as such the Prosecution is satisfied with that and believes that the sentence of 15 to 20 years is a fair and just sentence. I would like to explain in more detail during my closing remarks on that particular point. It's just been pointed out Mr. Obrenovic does not have his earphones on, and I think it is, of course, important that he hears the words of the Prosecutor. We've got another set of earphones over here if we need them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, would you please pause for a minute. I think there's some technical problems. Mr. Obrenovic, can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Everything is fine now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. You may sit down, please. Well, I'm sorry to interrupt you, Mr. McCloskey. Would you please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. If I could just briefly repeat to Mr. Obrenovic that we are here today because he was able to stand up in this courtroom and take responsibility for his actions and the actions of his unit, and it is the Prosecution's belief that he has fully cooperated with this office and has been truthful and credible in all respects and that I would like to go into more detail regarding his cooperation during my closing remarks. But I will, first of all, give a brief accounting of some of the evidence that we have provided this Chamber to outline some of the events that are most important in understanding this case so that the Court may best review those matters and sentence this individual. I will not go over the three witnesses that I've discussed in a previous hearing. That's part of our submissions, and we fully stand by all our submissions, and where we have stated succinctly and I believe very clearly our position, and I will stand by that today. The three people that I will not be referring to are -- one is Teufika Ibrahamefendic, who has provided a clear record on the impact of the victims; then we have Witness I from the Krstic trial, who is a survivor of the Branjevo Farm execution; and then Witness DD, who is one of the mothers of Srebrenica. We do have two other survivors of the mass executions in Zvornik, and I will briefly remind Your Honours of this crime by just taking a moment to go over some of the events. By the afternoon, evening of the 13th July, we know from one of the survivors that they begin to be moved up into buses from the town of Bratunac up to Zvornik, and the first known delivery of prisoners to the Zvornik Brigade is done in the evening hours at the Orahovac school, not far from Zvornik, where several hundred, 500 to 1.000 Muslims were eventually stored and killed the next day. Also in the evening hours of the 13th, the original evidence in this case saw a change of the post at the forward command post, where Drago Nikolic, the Chief of Security, in the late evening hours was moved to another job, an unknown job at that time, to deal with at that time, we felt, was probably prisoners and we pointed that out clearly in Mr. Butler's report. We now know, thanks to Mr. Obrenovic, exactly what that was about, as he has told us, and that he received a call from Drago Nikolic, who had been informed about the operation or the transfer of thousands of men to Zvornik would be occurring beginning that evening, and Mr. Obrenovic has acknowledged that he gave the authority to Drago Nikolic to begin the process of separating those men, detaining those men, and killing those men. He has stood and admitted that clearly, concisely, with no excuse. And it provides me and the Office of the Prosecutor a tremendous value to be able to get up and say this to you that clearly, and he is the one that took that responsibility and finally admitted this, and that's important. But what continued after he provided the authorisation, and as he said, he knew that it was in the area of 3.000 men, what continued the following day is more thousands of men came up, some 500 to 1.000 were shipped into the Petkovci school not far from Zvornik where they stayed the evening of the 14th, and were taken out the late night hours of the 14th, early morning hours of the 15th, to the site of dam not far away and systematically murdered. On that same day, on the 15th -- excuse me, on the 14th and early hours of the 15th, some 500 to 1.000 men were taken to the Rocevic school, where on the 15th of July they were transported over to an area near Kozluk. Now, we don't have a survivor of that crime, but we know from forensics that it was between 500 and 1.000 people that were taken out to this area near the Drina River and systematically executed. We also know that on the 14th and 15th at least 1.500 to 2.000 men were transported to the area of Pilica. Some 1.000, perhaps 1.200 were stored at the school in Pilica on the 14th and 15th and perhaps roughly 500, perhaps more, were stored in the cultural centre in the town of Pilica. On the 16th of July, members of the VRS, including members of the Zvornik Brigade, who were guarding these people at the school, took part in a process by which these 1.200 men at the Pilica school were taken to the Branjevo Military Farm and systematically killed. Then later that day some 500 or more men were killed inside the Pilica cultural centre in the centre of town. We may never know the true numbers involved, but our forensics and the information we have indicates it could be anywhere from 5.000 to 6.000 men that were killed in the Zvornik area at this time, perhaps more. And we know from the facts of the case, from the evidence presented, and from Mr. Obrenovic's own testimony that he was in command on the 13th of July and on the 14th of July and on the midday of the 15th of July, and was the person that must bear the command responsibility as the person that Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. authorised this in this Zvornik Brigade, as he has done so. After that, he took his position as chief of staff and was present during the combat operations and, of course, the operations to murder the men in the area. And we know from the evidence from Mr. Obrenovic himself that there was a large operation to hide and rebury the bodies in September, and that was such a crime on such a massive scale that I am reluctant to even describe it any more to you than what it was, because by those words I may diminish it and the victims that suffered so much. But I know this Court knows about this crime, knows about this case. And one of the reasons the Court can be so confident in its knowledge of the true nature and horror and responsibility in this case is because of what Mr. Obrenovic has had the ability and the courage to get up and do, and that is take responsibility for this crime and face a very significant sentence. As I said, Your Honour, I will save my more detailed description of his cooperation for my final statement, and I would leave you just with the words that this crime -- that we haven't seen anything in Europe since World War II like this, and it will obviously take very careful consideration and judgement and analysis on your part as you deliberate in this very important case. And I know you will do that, and I appreciate that. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could I now turn to Defence counsel for their opening statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Judge Argibay, Judge Vassylenko. We will waive any opening statement in the sense of discussing the facts of the case and the evidence; we would prefer to save that for our closing statement. By way of introduction to what we will be presenting to the Court today, we have four witnesses, as the Court is aware from our witness list. Two of those witnesses, we have asked that they appear in closed session for reasons that are in our pleadings. We also will be offering a number of exhibits. We filed an exhibit list with the Court on the 28th. These are all exhibits with one exception, which we have previously attached to pleadings in the case. After the witnesses have testified and after the Court has disposed of our request to admit the exhibits and after Mr. McCloskey and I have argued, Mr. Obrenovic has asked to address the Court at the conclusion of these proceedings. And so with that, at this point I would have nothing else to mention, unless the Court has questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, Mr. McCloskey, at this stage could I make sure that you don't have any live witnesses in these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. In order to, well, spare those people from having to come through this again, and because there is a very clear record from the Krstic trial and then because of the Court's knowledge in this matter and the nature of the entire proceedings, the Prosecution has not felt that that was necessary and we do not have any live witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And do you have any documents to tender into the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, regarding documents, no. But as in the previous matter, I should make clear - and I have discussed this with Defence counsel - we would be offering the testimony of Mr. Obrenovic in his trial at the Blagojevic/Jokic trial for your consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I guess there's no objections from the Defence team, so that transcript of the testimony of Mr. Obrenovic is admitted into the evidence. Mr. McCloskey, do you have any objections to the protective measures asked by the Defence concerning the two witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. We have discussed this and agree that, out of an abundance of caution, it's the safest way to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. So the request of protective measures for those witnesses are granted. Mr. Wilson, at this stage, do you have any documents to tender into evidence? You may tender it through the witness or you may tender it through 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, we have documents which are listed on our exhibit list filed on the 28th of October. The first nine exhibits, DS1 through DS9, are in fact 92 bis statements. The first eight of those are attached to our sentencing brief and the ninth one is attached to the witness list which we filed on the 28th. So we would offer those under the provisions of Rule 92 bis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. I guess there's no objections from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Those documents are admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Your Honour, in addition to the 92 bis exhibits, we have DS10 through DS17, which we've listed, and explained on our witness list. These are all documents which we believe are self-authenticating and which we believe the Prosecution has no objection to. All of these documents are attached to our pleadings, either through our sentencing brief or to our supplemental sentencing brief. And so at this time we would ask the Court to take those, pursuant to the permission in Rule 100(A), as we understand it, which allows the Court to consider any things that might be of assistance in the sentencing. So we would not be offering these through any witnesses, we would be offering these at this point, with the understanding that the Prosecution has no objection to their admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, why don't we make a decision now and admit those two documents into evidence at this stage; do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that we should admit those two documents into the evidence at this stage, rather than as an attachment to the --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And we would ask that they be labelled DS10 through DS17, as set out on the exhibit list. We've talked to the registrar and I understand it can be done in that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I see no objections from the Prosecution, so those two documents are admitted into the evidence. Mr. Wilson, are you ready to call your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: We are, Your Honour. Mr. Slijepcevic has the first witness, and he will be called at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So there's no protective measures concerning this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Not the first witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you make the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. THE WITNESS: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Slijepcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLIJEPCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon to the Prosecution and to everyone in the courtroom. Questioned by Mr. Slijepcevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you please, first of all, tell us your full name, your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: My name is Zorica Rikic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us your date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 17th of November, 1953.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your nationality and what is your religion? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I'm a Bosniak, and my religion is Orthodox.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you be so kind as to tell us where you were born.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I was born in Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you leave your place of birth and why?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I left my place of birth in 1979 for the sake of employment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you find employment?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I found employment in the same company in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when did you work there?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I worked in Sarajevo until 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your job?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I was a tradeswoman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the staff in your company of -- did they come from various ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since 1979, until the time when the war broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, up until that time, had you had nationalistic problems of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you tell us when these problems started, if they did.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: These problems started in 1992, in the month of March.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did these problems arise?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: There were checkpoints, barricades. On my way back from work, I and others going back from work would be stopped and checked.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who set up those barricades?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: They were set up by the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And who at that time made up the Territorial Defence of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: It was made up of the Green Berets.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the Green Berets drawn only from the Muslim people?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what part of Sarajevo did you live in?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I lived in the Muslim part of the town of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until when did you live and work in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I lived there until May 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you left Sarajevo, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I went in the direction of Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your departure from Sarajevo safe, and how did you leave?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I left the city of Sarajevo with great difficulty on a truck, escorted by SFOR from Milici to Bratunac and Ljubovija and finally arrived in Mali Zvornik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you able to carry with you any of your belongings?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I didn't take anything. Only a bag and the slippers I wore at work, a small nylon bag. That was all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Little Zvornik in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from Mali Zvornik, did you go back to your native town of Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it in the same month that you left Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On your arrival in Zvornik, did you ever meet Mr. Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was this?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: This was in February 1994.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I remember this because that was when my father died. Dragan and Bojana came to my house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell Their Honours who Bojana is.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Bojana is Mr. Obrenovic's wife. She is a friend of my sister's. They worked together in a company.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you socialise with Dragan Obrenovic's wife before, before you met Mr. Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you were introduced to Dragan Obrenovic, did you begin socialising with him?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your relationship to Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I met Mr. Obrenovic as a professional officer who was ten years my junior, but I respected him as if he were older than me. When he came to the house I was in, I would go out of the house because I had respect for him. I was nervous in his presence. He seemed such a nice person, a professional soldier, and then when I got to know him better, I would stay at home when he came to visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In all your years of knowing Dragan Obrenovic, did you learn of his being a member of any political organisation or being involved in politics in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: I think that Dragan Obrenovic was not a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During those same years, did you sometimes hear that Mr. Dragan Obrenovic exhibited any sort of nationalism or intolerance towards any other ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he socialise equally with all -- members of all ethnic groups in Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his opinion of so-called mixed marriages?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: His attitude to that was normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What do you mean when you say "normal"?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: His attitude to that was normal. Your Honours, I'll tell you one thing: I have a daughter living in Munich. She's a qualified nurse. She lives in a large clinic for women. She left in 1991. She married a black man. They live in Munich. She had a son with him called Kevin. And when she did this, I found it very difficult. She said, "You can all renounce me, but I love him and I will do it." That's when I got to know Bojana and Mr. Obrenovic and I complained to them. I said, "Dragan, look what my daughter's doing." And they said, "But they're young. They're in love. They have a child." And when they came to visit, this child played with the son of Mr. Obrenovic. They would stay with me a month, a month and a half, and they would play with little Milos, Dragan's son. Everything in Dragan's family was normal.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is your daughter-in-law a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes, she's a Croat.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is Dragan Obrenovic's attitude to her?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Normal, nice. My brother, Zoran --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises; it's her sister-in-law, not her daughter-in-law.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: They loved and respected Dragan a lot. My brother also lives in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLIJEPCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that a relative of Dragan Obrenovic's wife is also a Croat?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes.Q. Do you know that in 1996 the boyfriend of that relative's daughter would come to Zvornik and visit Dragan Obrenovic's house wearing an HVO uniform and that Dragan Obrenovic would escort him from his flat to the point of exit from Tuzla?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA RIKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The young man's name is Adam, and I know him and I know this relative of Mr. Obrenovic's wife.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLIJEPCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have a request now. May with go into private session for the next question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, may I say something?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please, witness, you may say something.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I want to tell you something very important today. My brother lives in Germany, and we have a restaurant in my house which my brother opened. And there was a time when my brother used to bring cars in from Germany, he would import them. And he imported a beautiful Mercedes, and he said, "I wish I could sell this to Mr. Obrenovic." And Dragan came, looked at it, and said, "Zoran, a Mercedes is Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. a nice car, but I can't take it. My people don't have enough bread to eat." I can never forget this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, witness. We'll go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. McCloskey, do you have any questions to this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence. We appreciate it very much. The usher will show you out of the room and we wish you to have a good journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Wilson, any protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: There are, Your Honour. This is one of the witnesses for whom we ask protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: We ask for a closed session for the next witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.[Trial Chamber and registrar confer]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We'll go to the private session, please.-- we'll go to the closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes. Mr. Slijepcevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLIJEPCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Questioned by Mr. Slijepcevic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mrs. Boskovic.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to thank you for having come to The Hague and having agreed to testify before this Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you don't understand any of my questions or if there are technical problems of any kind, please feel free to say so and interrupt me. Could you please tell this Trial Chamber your first and last name.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Dusanka Boskovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Boskovic, when were you born?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 19th of February, 1955 in Jegenov Lug, the municipality of Kalesija, which is about 20 kilometres from Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were the inhabitants of your place of birth only Serbs, or were they of mixed ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: The inhabitants were only of Serb nationality.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the surrounding villages, the villages surrounding your place of birth, who lived there? I am referring to the population of those Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. villages.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Muslims lived in those villages.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until when did you live in your place of birth?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: I lived in my place of birth until the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Boskovic, when did you get married?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 8th of February, 1975.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true to say that you have two sons?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you tell us their names and when they were born.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: The name of my first son is Sladjan Boskovic. He was born on the 10th of August, 1976. The name of my second son is Zoran Boskovic, and he was born on the 22nd of April, 1980.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is your profession, Mrs. Boskovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: I am a tradesman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you work until the 8th of April, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the 8th of May, 1992, I worked in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your job and in what sort of company were you employed?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: It was a state-owned company called Univerzal Promet Tuzla, Univerzal Trade Tuzla. And I was employ there had as a tradesman.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the staff employed in your company, were they of mixed ethnic origin, Serbs, Muslims who work there had?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Up until the 8th of May, 1992, had you had any sort -- any problems, problems of any kind on account of nationalistic feelings?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Up until the 8th of May, 1992, up until that period we had been involved in preparations. We had evacuated the children and older women from the village. So on the 7th of May, I went to work, and in the evening of the 7th I was told not to return home and that on the 8th of May all our people had to leave the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did these problems first appear, and what were the reasons?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: This first happened when --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to object. I don't know what the relevance of the beginnings and the reasons of this conflict are, and I really do not want to have to cross-examine on that point should certain reasons come out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a -- I don't see how it's relevant to this hearing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Slijepcevic, I think you have to concentrate on the subject of this hearing, which is your client's character and past behaviour. It has nothing to do with the conflict, unless -- unless those conflict is closely related to the matter I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLIJEPCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I just wanted to bring the witness to talk about Zvornik. I didn't want to create an unpleasant situation. I just wanted to show you how the witness got to Zvornik. That's why I was asking these questions. But if you don't think that this is necessary, then I will avoid asking them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please. Let's come to Zvornik as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLIJEPCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mrs. Boskovic, have I understood you correctly? Did you say that on the 7th of May, 1992 someone told you that you should not return home?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. My husband conveyed this message to me through a woman who was leaving on the 7th, and I was told not to return home.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do then?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: I worked in Tuzla until the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did you do on the 15th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: I then headed home, and I met a Muslim neighbour of mine who told me that we should leave the place, that some troops had arrived. She doesn't even know where these troops were from, which troops these were, but she said she couldn't help me to leave there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during that period of time, were you aware of the whereabouts of your husband?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did you go on the 15th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: On the 15th of May, I left with a cousin of mine from Tuzla. We went to Cakovici, where my older son was staying.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And from there?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: And from there, I went to Bijeljina on the 16th of May, with my son and cousin. My son and I continued from Bijeljina to Zvornik to find my husband there. When I arrived in Zvornik, I took my eldest son to a relative in Serbia. I returned to Veleki Zvornik again to look for my husband. And they told us that we couldn't contact them, that they were healthy and alive, they had got out on the 8th of May. I couldn't see him or speak to him for a month. Then when he came, we reached agreement and we went to Germany with the two children in June 1992. As he stayed on there on his own, we had contact; we would speak to each other while I was in Germany. He asked me to return with the children; he asked me to return to Zvornik. In October 1992, I returned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, did you see your husband, and where did you live with him?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: He met us there, and we lived in a house in which there were five other families. It was one room. There was one room with the four of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was your husband a member of the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What happened to your husband?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: He returned there and later on we saw each other on one other occasion. And on the 19th of December, he came to see us in Zvornik and he said that the line had been penetrated and about 130 people had been killed or had gone missing and that he had to leave. He left at that point, and he told us, "Take care of yourselves. I don't know how long I will be." So on the 21st of December, some people appeared and informed us of his death.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 21st of December, 1992, did you know Mr. Dragan Obrenovic?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. The mothers who had been widowed, we needed assistance from someone. We didn't know from whom, but we turned -- we appealed to the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the army provide you with any assistance? And who did so on behalf of the army?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: They told us that we should turn to Dragan Obrenovic, and they told us that we should not all go together but that only a few of us should go to talk to him. They said that they would provide us with assistance that we needed. I was the first to go. It had to do with my husband's funeral, clothes, food, et cetera. With regard to all these matters, the army did provide us with assistance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the course of 1993, did you receive any aid from Dragan Obrenovic or a representative of the army?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. For as long as we needed help, we were provided with help on a monthly basis. And if we were short of anything, we would receive the missing goods.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Among the group of 130 widows, were there any Muslim women?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I appeared in Zvornik, but I don't know those people, the inhabitants. People said that they were Muslims, and Muslims would socialise with us in 1992 and 1993, the Muslims who had remained in Zvornik. There were three orphans there, and we would provide them with some of the aid too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dragan Obrenovic make any kind of distinction on the basis of nationality?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: No. He never asked us whom we gave this assistance to. He never asked us what the names of the people who would receive assistance were. He said, "Provide those who need assistance with assistance."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Dragan Obrenovic ever help you as far as your flat is concerned?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. In 1992, when my husband was killed, I moved into a flat which Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. had been taken by a man. I moved into that flat with two children. Someone from the army started maltreating me, and I went to find Dragan Obrenovic to ask him for assistance again, as we had no one else to turn to. He sent a soldier to see me who said, "Just choose who's going to come, so that we know, because this can't happen again. It must not happen again." And then later on it was a little easier for us, since we benefited from someone's support. The most difficult time was in 1994, when my older son was finishing school. I didn't have enough money to buy him a suit, and so Dragan told me to go to his flat and to take whatever my son needed. We went to his flat. He gave him his suit, shirts, ties, shoes, socks. He gave him everything so that he could go to a graduation ceremony with his -- with his circle of friends.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you at any time hear of Dragan Obrenovic having demonstrated hatred towards members of the Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: DUSANKA BOSKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SLIJEPCEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Any questions, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, witness, thank you very much for coming to The Hague to give your evidence in these proceedings, and please accept our sympathy to your sufferings during that time. The usher will show you out of the room, and we wish you a pleasant journey back home. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I understand that the next witness is a protected witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And the -- my suggestion is that we have a 20-minute break and during this time I hope that we'll make the necessary arrangements for the next witness, and we will start in the closed session, as I understand. And Ms. Stewart, would you please move your cart away to makesome room for the next witness; during the break, I mean. So we will resume at quarter to 5.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. McCloskey, any closing argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. Mr. President, Your Honours, Mr. Obrenovic, as the deputy commander of a brigade in wartime and as the man in command of the Zvornik Brigade at the time, bears one of the most awesome responsibilities in human endeavours. A military commander has the power of life and death in his hands; he has the power of protecting his own village, his town, his women and children. And of course, as we know, he has the power and responsibility over those in his custody. This is an awesome power, and an even more awesome responsibility. Mr. Obrenovic has stood in this court and looked us in the eye and taken responsibility for the murder of thousands of individuals. What possible sentence can there be for such a crime? But the value to the Prosecution in this case is immense, and it's immense because this man was able to stand up and take that responsibility as a commander, the first commander in this war that I'm aware that was able to do this. And I'll explain to you why that is so valuable, why that is so important, both historically to the former Yugoslavia and to this Tribunal. In 1998, I was part of a team that searched the Zvornik Brigade. I met with Mr. Obrenovic in his office. He waited for the orders of his commanders, and when he got them, he cooperated with us fully. I saw him brief his troops and his staff, and for the next eight to ten hours we had full cooperation and were able to do our job and do our duty without fear, without any problem at all. All we had with us was one major from the United States Army with a sidearm. At that time, I naively saw something in the character of Mr. Obrenovic that I hoped that may some day do the right thing, and today we know he has, and that was much appreciated. But I think it's on a larger scale that Mr. Obrenovic has provided the truth regarding Srebrenica in a simple, clear, articulate fashion, as the commander in charge of one of the most gruesome days in this war. Now, as I've stated before, bringing the truth to the former Yugoslavia, bringing it to the Muslim community and to the Serb community, has historical repercussions and helps us in our duty for peace and reconciliation. We know that from the responses of Muslim leaders and Muslim individuals, many of whom I know that feel this incredible sense of relief that the truth has finally been told by someone of unquestionable military responsibility and character, character in a military sense but not, unfortunately, in the sense of honour that it took at the time to walk away from this. He obviously did not do that; he did not do the right Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. thing. He chose instead to do what his superiors had ordered him to do in what unfortunately had been a part of this war ever since 1992. But he brings to us today and to the former Yugoslavia and to this Tribunal some hope that reconciliation can happen, that soldiers of his rank can tell the truth and will come forward and will provide some basis for reconciliation. We've seen some of the character of the individuals from the former Yugoslavia in this court today, and that gives us hope that they will take what he has started and take that home with him. And importantly, what does he bring this Tribunal in this particular case? Well, you saw his recounting of the events. You saw the way he answered me questions, the way he is answered Mr. Karnavas's questions, Ms. Sinatra's questions, clearly, concisely, without hesitation, and most importantly without excuse. And I've not heard any excuses today or anything that would lead me to believe that he has not accepted his responsibility. This came across in court clear, and it came across with the kind of strength and the kind of value that a Prosecutor rarely sees in a situation with a cooperating witness. It's the kind of evidence that you will be able to take back to you in your chambers and review word by word, and unless I'm mistaken, you'll be able to count on it. You'll see the rest of the evidence in this case and you'll be able to compare it, and that will be of incredible value to you as the triers of the fact. And I have no doubt that Mr. Obrenovic will testify the same way in the upcoming Srebrenica trials and I'm confident there will be some. Serbia must now look to what is going on in this Tribunal, and they will see the truth. They will see fellow Serbs standing up, like Mr. Nikolic and Mr. Obrenovic. And I have again naive hopes that that will in some way help them, officials there in that country that I believe are harbouring most of the serious accused in this case. And I know Mr. Obrenovic will stand by his word and testify in those manners -- in those matters, like he did in the case before us. And in particular, you have had the benefit of hearing from a VRS commander, brigade commander on military issues of command and control and responsibility. This is an incredibly unique perspective you're getting. The brigade in any army, and I think especially in the VRS, commanded the men that were in the trenches. This was the vast majority of the men. These are the men that, on both sides, fought and died. The commander of the brigade is the one that has the responsibility for those men and for the men under his custody. And we were able to hear from such a commander and hear about his responsibility as a commander. And despite a rigorous and difficult cross-examination, he never wavered from his responsibility as commander and was able to show you what that meant much more than could possibly be told from the regulations or from even the experts of the Prosecution. This is of tremendous value, and it will be so in the future. He was especially able to tell us - and I'm not going to go into the detail on this; it's not appropriate at this time - but he was able to tell us about the security branch and how the security branch worked in the command and to dispel some myths in that regard. As Your Honours know, he also brought to this case materials, original materials, and I have explained in detail to this Court the value of those materials. So when we look at this awful, awful crime, you will ask yourselves - I know you will; I know you probably already have - What possible sentence can there be? But I ask you to look into this recommendation of the Prosecutor, 15 to 20 years, and see that it's reasonable because of the value that this man has provided this Prosecution. There was a day when we stood at the base of the dam at Petkovci with four survivors and huge mass graves in forensic reports and that was it. We're no longer at that stage, and that is to the benefit of this Tribunal, to the benefit of the former Yugoslavia, and I know to the benefit of many Muslims that find great relief in seeing the truth so clearly said. Now, my words today and Mr. Obrenovic's words and your judgement cannot bring back the dead and it cannot assuage the grief and the misery of the women and surviving men of Srebrenica. But I still have some of the naive hopes I had that day in 1998, when we searched the Zvornik Brigade. I think this process that we have entered into and this plea agreement that you have accepted as a review is a very important part of this process, and I trust and I know you will give it your most valued consideration. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. McCloskey. [Trial Chamber confers]JUDGE LIU: Well, Mr. Wilson, do you have any closing argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: I do, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, Judge Argibay, Judge Vassylenko, Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Waespi, and staff, Mr. Slijepcevic and I appreciate the opportunity to speak to you on behalf of our client, Dragan Obrenovic. We've had the privilege of representing him for two and a half years during which time he has struggled with trying to resolve the serious charges against him, in trying to reach a resolution of those charges extremely which was appropriate -- I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, please go slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Because the transcript cannot correctly reflect what you said.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: And make a pause after every sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: My apologies. I was saying, Your Honour, that we've had the privilege of representing Mr. Obrenovic for two and a half years. We're honoured that he chose us as his lawyers representing him and helping him as he struggled to resolve the extremely serious charges against him and to find a solution that was not only good for him but was also an appropriate solution for the tortured country which he honourably fought for and bled for, has been the professional highlight of the legal careers of myself and Mr. Slijepcevic. We have come to know him as a man of unusual courage, intellect, and commitment. We submit that you have seen those same qualities demonstrated here in your courtroom. We've provided you with two briefs of the subject of sentencing, and I'm not going to stand here this evening and try to go through those. I know that you will read them and study them and give them whatever weight they are due, and we will rest on those briefs as to the subjects that they're covering. What I would like to do this evening is to talk about two issues, two questions which I think that you must consider as you decide what is the appropriate sentence in this case. The first question is: Who is Dragan Obrenovic? The second question is: What should you do you with Dragan Obrenovic? When Mr. Obrenovic made the decision to plead guilty before you, one of the greatest fears of Mr. Slijepcevic and myself was that by pleading guilty at the beginning of the trial, before you had had a full understanding of the facts surrounding his role in these events and, in fact, the events themselves, that we would be at a terrible disadvantage when we came to the day, to the sentencing day. We explained to him that if he pleaded guilty before the trial started, the Trial Chamber would be faced possibly with sentencing him without knowing any of the following things: You would not know that the crimes in question took place while he was at the battle front, in active command of the army units in what the Prosecution experts refer to as pitched, hand- to-hand desperate combat with a vastly superior enemy force; you would not know that the crimes in question took place when he was still officially on convalescent leave, recovering from his earlier combat wounds. There were a whole host of facts in the complex matrix of conditions in Zvornik in July of 1995 that we believe that you would need to know in order to reach an appropriate sentence in this case. We explained to Mr. Obrenovic that even if he felt that he was guilty, he had a right to go to trial and require the Prosecution to prove his guilt Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. beyond a reasonable doubt. We explained to him that we could mount a very substantial defence to the charges, that he would have numerous witnesses who believed in him and who would testify as to his good character. We told him that if he were found guilty after a two-year trial that at that - -

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Defence counsel please slow down a bit for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Your Honour, I am from the southern US usually they tell me I speak too slowly, so I'll work on that. We told him that if he were found guilty after a two-year trial, that at that time the Trial Chamber would have a much better understanding of his role in these offences and you would be in a better position to determine his sentence. We stress that we felt that a better understanding of the case and of his role in it was that it would be very much to his benefit at any sentencing hearing. There came a time, however, when Mr. Obrenovic thanked us for our legal advice, but pointed out that he had a moral decision to make which was his alone and that he had decided that he didn't want to contest the charges. We agreed with him that ultimately that decision was his and his alone to make. He asked us to approach Mr. McCloskey in open negotiations with the goal of his pleading guilty. We did so, and that process resulted in us being here today. As we address you today, we are relieved that while you haven't had two years' exposure to this case, that you have had an opportunity to -- a substantial opportunity to fairly acquaint yourselves with the basic facts of Srebrenica and with the role played by Mr. Obrenovic in those facts. You know what he did do, but you also know what he did not do. You know what he did, and you know what the numerous other individuals who are fugitives from these charges did. Those individuals include his entire chain of command, even its civilian president. Almost all of those individuals remain fugitives from justice, hiding in the hills of the Balkans, leaving their people to face the world's opprobrium, which has naturally and inevitably flowed from the enormity of their misconduct. You have also had at least some opportunity to get to know the accused, Dragan Obrenovic, the man, as a person. He has appeared before you for almost seven full days of testimony, including rigorous cross-examination by other Defence teams and examinations by Your Honours. We believe that the Prosecution is correct when they note in their brief the following things: That it is "absolutely clear that he provided truthful and complete testimony at the trial; that his testimony was extraordinary in its objectivity, clarity, and integrity; that he testified without hesitation or excuse as to his own acts; that he strived to answer all of the questions truthfully and completely without regard to who asked the questions and without regard to whether the truth helped or hurt any party in the case." In sum, as the Prosecution said, the record speaks for itself and nowhere in that record does the Prosecution find any reason to doubt the testimony of Dragan Obrenovic. Moreover, as Mr. McCloskey has pointed out and as he has repeated this evening, Mr. Obrenovic has provided the Prosecution with something that they have not had before in addressing these cases, and that has his military expertise. He is a person who can explain to the Tribunal, to the triers of fact, the extensive military communications, structures, policies, and manoeuvres which you need to understand in addressing this case. We attached to our brief -- the latest brief -- a copy of the Wall Street Journal editorial noting that "Finally the Tribunal appears to be getting credible testimony which will allow it to move forward on the issue of Srebrenica." We submit that it is beyond question that Mr. Obrenovic has provided substantial cooperation to the Prosecution and to the Tribunal in accomplishing its mission. In doing so, he has clearly met the criteria for establishing mitigation under the Rules of this Court. But if he has mitigated his conduct by pleading guilty and by providing substantial assistance to the Tribunal, we still recognise that you are faced with answering those two questions with which I began my remarks: Who ultimately is Dragan Obrenovic and what should you do with him? We'd like to devote the remainder of our argument to trying to answer these questions. As you know from the witnesses appearing on his behalf, both in Rule 92 bis statements and live here today, he was never a bigoted person or an individual known for mistreating anyone, prisoner or otherwise. You've heard and read the statements of people from both the Serbian and the Muslim community as to individual acts of kindness and courage and a general reputation as a decent human being. Others who could relate similar experiences exist, but did not feel free to come forward. We understand their predicament. We submit to you that the question of who is Dragan Obrenovic and how did he come before you is o complex one. It's complex because Dragan Obrenovic, like everybody else in this courtroom and in the world in which we all exist, is a complex individual. He has strengths and yet weaknesses; he has courage, and at the same time, he has fears. He has noble instincts and yet obviously he has human failings. He's a man with admirable humility, yet at the same time he has a mixture of the pride and ambition which accompanies every successful man and woman and which on occasion leads to our undoing. The Nobel Laureate, William Faulkner, who wrote about a section of my native country known for its own ethnic and racial problems, once said in one of his novels that "no man living or dead is much better than any other man living or dead." I read that passage as a young man, and I never forgot it. I've kept a copy of it during the 37 years I have been a lawyer trying criminal cases in one role or another. I've often returned to that for the simple yet profound truth that it expresses: That we are all imperfect beings, that we are all humans, with all that includes. If you put Dragan Obrenovic under a microscope, he like all the rest of us would turn out to be a complex being, a mixture of the contrasting and conflicting forces that is exist in all of us. By all accounts, until July 13th, 1995, Mr. Obrenovic had for 32 careers lived an exemplary life. He had established a record of which all of us would be proud. Professionally, he represented the cream of the military elite. He was a young man who through his intellect, courage, and natural abilities would have risen to the top of any army in the world. He was a man who was all first among equals in any setting, from his place in his nation's military academy to positions of increasing responsibility. He was admired and respected by his superiors and his subordinates alike and by the civilian community, which he served. He was a somewhat austere man who shunned the fancy cars, uniforms, and other trappings of his rank and position, all of which were his for the asking. He was, in short, a soldier's soldier. He was the type of officer of whom it is said in military circle, his men and women subordinates would have followed him down the barrel of a cannon. He was an officer who led by example, who was not an armchair commander but was always in the thick of battle, whose men knew that he would not ask them to do anything which he himself would not do. He was a man whose penchant for leading from the front led to his serious wounding in the months before Srebrenica, which in turn led to him being on the invalid list when that campaign began, a status he should never have abandoned. In any society, in any army, in any profession, including our own legal profession, young men and women of exceptional ability, like Dragan Obrenovic, are spotted by their elders and marked for great things. They are pushed along at a more rapid pace than their contemporaries. They are given responsibilities and promotions usually reserved for people who are older, more mature, more seasoned, and more experienced. They are any society's golden youth. They are the best we have to offer and our hopes for the future. We, their elders, take pride in our own roles in spotting young people like this and in forwarding and advancing their careers. They, in turn, are led to believe that they can do anything; that no task Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. is beyond their natural talents and abilities; that intellect and energy are all that's required; and that new and more challenging assignments are simply more opportunities to excel. This was the public Dragan Obrenovic in July 1995, a man who in one of my colleague's cross-examination was accurately described as being on the fast track for advancement in his army, a man who many thought walked on water. But in truth, he did not walk on water in July of 1995. Like the rest of us, for all his abilities and accomplishments, he was all too human and capable of succumbing to fear and failure and the other forces which confronted him, as Zvornik and his small temporary command threatened to fall to the enemy. So when we ask who is Dragan Obrenovic and who was he in July 1995, the answer doesn't end with a list of his remarkable accomplishments to that day and the endorsements of those who knew him, because in addition to that, he was all too human. He was a 32- year-old junior officer who had finally been pushed by his superiors into a position where he was over his head. The military had finally been pushed by his superiors into a position where he was over his head, a military position which the Prosecution called in their opening statement an untenable one, a position in which he could not win. But because he was Dragan Obrenovic, he also could not say no when he was asked to help. When called upon by those military superiors to leave his sickbed and temporarily assume command of part of his brigade in battle, some deadly combination of a sense of duty, hubris, ambition, pride or whatever kept him from saying no. As always he rose to the challenge. But this time he did not move mountains, he failed spectacularly. Given pathetically inadequate forces with which to confront an overwhelming enemy descending upon him from two directions, he threw himself into the struggle, denied permission by his superiors to allow the more powerful Muslim 28th Division to pass through his lines, he fought with what he had. Given the impossible order for more mature generals to destroy the column, he was ridiculed by them for being terrified and pointing out to them that both his small command in the city of Zvornik faced annihilation. He watched helplessly as his own soldiers began to die by the dozens. He fled his command post one step ahead of the enemy, leaving behind his dead and wounded. And into this tableau comes the mad and atrocious plan by his military and civilian leaders to massacre prisoners, a plan hatched, organised, and executed by these so-called leaders from the comfort and security of their own well-guarded headquarters. He has told that this has been ordered from the very highest levels of the army and his government. It is a claim now established by the list of indictments obtained by the Prosecution in the area of Srebrenica. He was told in effect that you yourself "don't have to get your hands dirty, you can continue fighting your battles," but we'll need to borrow some of your MPs and then we'll need to borrow some of your bulldozer drivers to dig the graves, and he should also have foreseen that they might also borrow other people from the Zvornik Brigade to guard prisoners and help out in the logistics. And what did Dragan Obrenovic do when he was faced with this most important test of his life? The young man who could not fail, failed spectacularly. He gave them what they wanted. He directed his own attention to the vastly more acceptable task of fighting the impossible battle. When asked on the witness stand, "Why did you not protest," Dragan Obrenovic admitted what for him must have been one of his most painful admissions, "I was afraid." Given the positions of those people who ordered and carried out the Srebrenica massacres, it's a logical question for any of us studying this case to ask, What would have happened if he had said no to their request for assistance in their gruesome job? Could Major Obrenovic, on the front lines in the hills of Snagovo, have faced down President Karadzic and General Mladic and everyone else up the chain of command? Would they have abandoned their massive crime entailing dozens if not hundreds of their subordinates if he had said no to the request for a dozen MPs or half a dozen MPs on July 13th? Who should he have turned to? His brigade commander? His corps commander? The commanding general of the army? His president? What would have happened to Dragan Obrenovic if he had said no? But in the end, all of these are rhetorical questions because it didn't happen that way, and in defence of himself, Mr. Obrenovic has never asked anyone to speculate for him. Instead, in the words of the Prosecution, he "has always taken responsibility for his actions and he has never offered excuses for his conduct." He did not claim, "There was nothing I could have done" or that "events were beyond my control." Rather, he confessed to the most human of failures: fear - and he has steadfastly accepted responsibility for the consequences of his failure. Nor, we might add, has he ever attempted to blame anyone else for his shortcomings. We respectfully submit to you that no one aware of his failings during those days than Dragan Obrenovic. He is his own worst judge. He knows the impact of his failure more than anyone. He has already sentenced himself. He is like Lady MacBeth, sentenced forever to the Sisyphean task of constantly washing her hands in a futile attempt to erase an indelible stain. And when you ask who is Dragan Obrenovic, you must also take into account his origins and the society from which he came and the special problems of that society, because here again, we are all shaped by our environment and the communities we grew up in. His environment and community was that of Bosnia. As a result of the 1992-1995 war, much has been written about Bosnia in the last decade. Many people who could not have identified it on the map before that event at least have a general impression of it as a tortured land located at one of the world's great cultural crossroads. Others know it from the great literary works of Bosnia's Nobel laureate, Ivo Andric, who told its epic story in his work "The Bridge on the Drina." Andric's great novel, spanning four centuries, provides an unforgettable, uplifting, and ultimately hopeful tapestry of his beautiful country, but Andric was also aware of its darker side, just below the surface. In a letter to a friend in 1920, he wrote the following words: "Perhaps in Bosnia people should be warned everywhere and on every occasion to be aware of hatred, inborn, unconscious, endemic hatred, because in that land shared by four nations and four faiths, four times as much love and mutual sympathy is required as in any other land." Would that Ivo Andric have stood beside Dragan Obrenovic to have whispered in his ear, "Beware...Beware." And so we come to the second ultimate question here today: What should you do with Dragan Obrenovic? Knowing, as he did, that he was to be charged with the role in the crimes of Srebrenica, Dragan Obrenovic had three choices: He could join all of the other accused individuals who remained free and beyond the reach of this Tribunal. Theirs is a precarious existence, yet all of us know that there is a substantial chance that many, if not most of them, will never see The Hague. Many of these who actually planned the executions, actually ordered them, and even pulled the triggers remain free in the Balkans. In the eyes of many of their countrymen, they enjoy the status of heroes and they enjoy the active support of many of those citizens. Dragan Obrenovic had this option when he realised that Mr. McCloskey and his forces were zeroing in on him. He did not flee. He could have contested the charges against him and drug out the issue of his guilt for several more years. Here again he would have enjoyed the continuing status of a hero among many of his fellow countrymen, and if he had been ultimately convicted, he would have been viewed by those same people as not only a hero but now a victim of The Hague. And when, on some future distant date, after he had served whatever sentence given him, he would have returned home and he would have been welcomed back as a hero and a victim by some of those same people. He declined the option of denying his guilt. Instead, he pleaded guilty to his own involvement in the events of Srebrenica and agreed to cooperate with the Tribunal in its efforts to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. fairly affix responsibility for what happened in July of 1995. Having rejected two courses of action, which would have made him a hero to many in his home country, he chose a course of action which consigned him to a very different status with those same people; it is a very hard road that he has chosen. In accepting responsibility and cooperating with the Tribunal, Mr. Obrenovic is doing what he can to balance the book of his life. His remorse is genuine. His intentions are to meet his obligations under the plea agreement without reservations, as the Prosecution's note in their brief and in their comments here today. We submit to the Trial Chamber that as human beings, repentance and forgiveness are of the loftiest heights to which human spirits can aspire. None of us can completely insulate ourselves from his or her surroundings in the presses and circumstances of the moment in which he or she finds himself or herself. It's easy for me now, at roughly twice Dragan Obrenovic's age in 1995, to sit in my study in Seattle and say what mistakes I would never permit myself to make. But in the privacy of my innermost thoughts, I have remembered another young man who at 32 was also an officer in another army during another war in another part of the world. And I have asked myself if there were any imaginable circumstances that could ever have made that young man stumble, as did Dragan Obrenovic. And after knowing Mr. Obrenovic for two years, I'm no longer so sure of the answer. I'm delighted that that young man was never -- and relieved that the young man was never subjected to pressures like that. And I'm also delighted that I don't even have to answer the hypothetical question of: Were there such circumstances that could have caused that person to do that? There's an ancient Native American proverb that says one must walk in the moccasins of another person for two days before one can fully understand that person's actions and thoughts. Like many proverbs, it has stood the test of time because it has universal application. It's something we all recognise. No one can completely insulate himself from the pressures around him any more than he or she can step out of the confines of his own nature. More often than not, we're all somewhat cornered by our circumstances. But how one transcends those circumstances or fails to transcend them depends on him and him alone. Civilised society requires individual accountability. If one makes the right choice when others around him are headed down the wrong roads, then properly he becomes the hero to posterity. But if one makes the wrong choice, that's not the end of the matter. His responsibilities do not end and the book of his life is not yet closed. He still must decide what he's going to do about his mistake. Should he refuse to acknowledge it and fold himself into the comforting surroundings of others who have taken that -- made that mistake and are also refusing to acknowledge it, or should he confront that mistake, admit the mistake, repent, and strive to earn forgiveness? We submit that those who choose the latter road of repenting and seeking to remedy their wrongs and obtain forgiveness without question demonstrate an ability to overcome themselves. They also serve as models who provide inspiration and support for the rest of us, as each of us faces our own comparatively mundane crises. The Tribunal has of course recognised this on many cases, including the judgement of the Erdemovic case, also a case flowing from Srebrenica. When I sit down in just a few moments, the active roles of myself and my partner and my friend, Mr. Slijepcevic, before you will end. We have tried to represent Mr. Obrenovic in the manner and toward the goal which he has directed us. We have done our best for him. We will be tendering him now to you for your wise judgement. We tender you not a perfect man, because there aren't any of those. But neither is he an evil man. Instead, we submit to you that we present to you in the form of Dragan Obrenovic simply a good man with many fine qualities who, in the press of the much critical moment in his life, failed to live up to his own standards and those standards that are required by international law. Dragan Obrenovic is a man with many redeeming qualities. He has shown himself worthy of your mercy and deserving of an opportunity to salvage as much of his once-promising life as you're willing to give him. Whatever sentence you give him, he will make the most of it. Considering all of the facts and circumstances of the case but, most importantly, his role in the case, his remorse, his cooperation, and the other mitigating factors which we have set out in our brief, we ask that you sentence him to imprisonment for a period in the range of 8 to 12 years. It is a sentence which is appropriately severe given the facts before you which will send the appropriate message to those who need to hear that message and which is consistent with sentences in other cases, such as that of Erdemovic and Plavsic. In closing, Mr. Slijepcevic and I thank you for your courtesy and attention to us as lawyers, not only today but on every day in which we have been privileged to appear before you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Wilson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we understand that Mr. Obrenovic would like to make a statement. Mr. Obrenovic, you may make a statement. Please be seated while making the statement. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I am grateful to you for granting me leave to address you today. On the territory of the country in which I was born, shooting from firearms was usual when celebrating the birth of a male child. These shots tell you everything, what a new male member of the family means and what is expected of him - strength, protection; he should be a warrior, a soldier, the head of the family, as they say in our parts. Unfortunately, when other kinds of shooting started in the former Yugoslavia, shooting in war, it was normal for every man, every male child, to put on a uniform, take up a weapon, and go to protect his homeland, his nation, and ultimately his family. This was expected of him. This was his role, a sacred role. There was no choice. You could be either a soldier or a traitor. At the beginning of the war, it seemed as if the war and all it brought with it was impossible, that this wasn't really happening to us, and that everything would be resolved within a few days, and that finally our generation would have a chance. We didn't even notice how we were drawn into the vortex of inter-ethnic hatred and how neighbours were no longer able to live beside each other, how death moved into the vicinity, and we didn't even notice that we had got used to it. Death became our reality. Unfortunately, it became everyday reality. Who before that could have believed that the horrors of war would have become everyday reality? Who could have believed that they could become a part of our lives? Surrounded with horrors, we got used to them and went on living like that. Among those horrors, things happened that were done by people who knew each other, people who, until yesterday, had lived almost as family members together. In Bosnia, a neighbour means more than a relative. In Bosnia, having coffee with your neighbour is a ritual, and this is what we trampled on and forgot. We lost ourselves in hatred and brutality. And in this vortex of terrible misfortune and horror, the horror of Srebrenica happened. I am here before Your Honours because I wish to express my remorse. I have thought for a long time, and I'm always followed by the same thought - guilt. I find it very hard to say this truth. I am to blame for everything I did at that time. I am trying to erase all this and to be what I was not at that time. I am also to blame for what I did not do, for not trying to protect those prisoners. Regardless of the temporary nature of my then-post. I ask myself again and again, What could I have done that I didn't do? Thousands of innocent victims perished. Graves remain behind, refugees general destruction and misfortune and misery. I bear part of the responsibility for this. There is misfortune on all sides that stays behind as a warning that this should never happen again. My testimony and admission of guilt will also remove blame from my nation because it is individual guilt, the guilt of a man named Dragan Obrenovic. I stand by this. I am responsible for this. The guilt for this I feel remorse and for which I apologise to the victims and to their shadows, I will be happy if this contributed to reconciliation in Bosnia, if neighbours can again shake hands, if our children can again play games together, and if they have the right to a chance. I will be happy if my testimony helps the families of victims, if I can spare them having to testify again and thus relive the horrors and the pain during their testimony. It is my wish that my testimony should help prevent this ever happening again, not just in Bosnia, but anywhere in the world. It is too late for me now, but for the children living in Bosnia now, it's not too late and I hope that this will be a good warning to them. In our wartime sufferings, no one has come out as the victim; everybody is suffering now. On all sides, there is still pain. What has won the victory is misfortune and unhappiness, as a consequence of blind hatred. The spirit of this unhappiness still hovers over our Bosnian hills, which have suffered so much, and it will take years to wipe out the traces of this horrible war and to have smoke rise again from people's chimneys, from the hearths, and maybe decades will have to pass before the wounds in people's souls are healed. If my confession, my testimony, and my remorse, if my attempt to face myself contributes to the quicker healing of these wounds, I will have done my duty of a soldier, a fighter, a human being, and a father. In the end, I wish to thank the Prosecution for their efforts to establish the truth and for their efforts to have justice done. I would like to thank you, Your Honours, for listening to me so attentively throughout my testimony. I tried to answer every question put to me as correctly and truthfully as I could. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it seems to me that the Judges have no questions to put to Mr. Obrenovic after he made his statement. At this stage, are there any other matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Wilson?

utterances.speaker: MR. WILSON
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. This Trial Chamber will withdraw to elaborate the evidence admitted in these proceedings as well as the testimonies given by the witnesses today. In the meantime, the Chamber will issue an order instructing the Registrar to set a date for the delivering of the judgement before the winter recess, probably in December. Having said that, I declare that this hearing is closed.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.17 p.m.
